summary:
HALO (Health Assessment for Long-duration Operations) is an on-board health monitoring web app for astronauts on long missions, where medical advice from Earth can be many minutes away or cut off by a comms blackout.

What we developed: Each crew member unlocks their own record with a passcode and logs readings by guided timer, Bluetooth device, camera pulse or manual entry. HALO tracks 17 signals, from heart rate, sleep and mood to bone density, near vision, cabin CO2 and radiation dose. The 'Today' screen reduces them to one word (Normal, Watch or Urgent), one reason and one next step. On-board rules flag early fatigue, possible infection and rising blood sugar. Health Buddy, a rule-based assistant with no AI model, triages symptoms locally and answers from NASA Human Research Program material.

How it addresses the challenge: HALO runs in the browser with or without a ground link. Records are encrypted on board and sync when a link is up. It adapts to five mission settings, from space station to Mars base, and escalates to the Crew Medical Officer or the ground flight surgeon to suit the communication delay.

Why it matters: Far from Earth, crews must detect and manage health problems themselves. HALO gives every astronaut an early warning and a clear action, grounded in NASA’s published spaceflight risks and NASA-STD-3001, so small problems are handled before they become mission problems. HALO is a prototype with simulated data, not for clinical use.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

HALO (Health Assessment for Long-duration Operations) is an on-board health monitoring web app for astronauts. Each crew member picks their profile, unlocks their own encrypted record with a passcode, and logs readings by guided timer, Bluetooth device, camera pulse or manual entry. HALO tracks 17 signals: heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, blood oxygen, hydration, exercise, bone density change, near vision, vigilance lapses, fatigue, body mass, food energy, cabin CO2 and radiation dose.

Every reading is compared with a normal range and with the astronaut’s own pre-flight baseline. The Today screen then shows one word (Normal, Watch or Urgent), one reason and one next step. On-board rules combine trends across signals to flag early fatigue and stress, possible infection, and rising blood sugar. Alerts move through a lifecycle from open, to re-check, to escalated, to cleared by the Crew Medical Officer.

Health Buddy, the on-board assistant, triages typed or spoken symptoms with local protocols and answers questions about spaceflight risks from a built-in knowledge base. Other sections cover a body map, trends, a daily routine, training, an EVA go/no-go check, and a crew view for the Crew Medical Officer.

What benefits does it have?

  • It works with or without a link to Earth, so advice never waits on a signal.
  • It catches problems early, when several small changes point the same way.
  • It tells the astronaut what to do next, not only what the numbers are.
  • It keeps medical data private: records are encrypted with each astronaut’s passcode, and mood is shared with the medical officer only if the astronaut allows it.
  • It gives the Crew Medical Officer one inbox showing who needs attention first.

What is the intended impact?

As missions travel further from Earth, crews must detect and manage health problems themselves. HALO is meant to support that independence: small problems are noticed and handled on board before they become mission problems, and the ground receives a small health report whenever a link is available.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did we use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no front-end framework.
  • Browser features: Web Crypto for encryption (AES-GCM, PBKDF2, RSA-OAEP), IndexedDB for on-device storage, a service worker for offline use, speech recognition and speech output for Health Buddy, and Bluetooth and camera input for measurements.
  • Hosting: Vercel.
  • Hardware: none is required. HALO runs on any device with a modern browser and is designed to take readings from wearables, a blood pressure cuff, a pulse oximeter, a glucometer and a dosimeter.
  • NASA resources: the Human Research Program pages on spaceflight risks and hazards, NASA-STD-3001, and the PVT-B vigilance test from NASA’s Cognition battery.

How is the project creative?

  • The status block answers “how am I, why, and what now” in a single glance.
  • “Road to Mars” turns exercise into a journey: every training minute moves the astronaut’s ship 40,000 km, past the Moon and on toward Mars, with quests and badges.
  • Five mission settings (space station, Mars transit, lunar base, Mars base and rover) change the gravity, the exercise equipment, the communication delay and who gets called.
  • Health Buddy uses no AI model. Its advice comes from fixed protocols and NASA material, so every answer can be traced to its source.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Communication delay and blackouts, which is why everything runs on board.
  • Medical privacy within a small crew.
  • The cabin environment: a dark, low-glare screen for dim cabins and sleep periods, and large touch targets for gloved hands.
  • Accessibility: status colour always appears with an icon and a word.
  • Trust: rule-based logic that shows its reasons, in place of a model that cannot explain itself.
  • Slow links: a small report file made for limited bandwidth.
  • Honesty about limits: HALO is a prototype with simulated crew data, its thresholds are prototype values for review against NASA-STD-3001.
